 How to Watch the 2026 WTA Finals and ATP Finals (Even for Free)
 Updated Nov 14, 2026 
 The 2026 tennis season is coming to a close. Find out which singles and doubles players can be called the best as the WTA Finals conclude and the ATP Finals get started this weekend.

 After four Grand Slam titles and months of competition, it all comes down to this. The 2026 tennis season will culminate in the WTA Finals and ATP Finals to decide the best pro tennis players of the year. The top eight singles players and doubles teams from the WTA Tour and ATP Tour will come together in November to compete in a round-robin tournament before moving on to the semifinals and finals. This weekend, the women's tournament will conclude with the seminfinals and finals. The singles and doubles competitions for the ATP Finals will also begin. Which of the sport's best players will prevail? Here's how to catch the action live. WTA Finals and ATP Finals Schedule
 While the WTA Finals and ATP Finals take place back-to-back, they are technically separate events held in different locations. The women's finals will be held first from Nov. 8-15 . The 2026 WTA Finals will take place at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden in Indian Wells, California. It was initially intended to be played in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, but the venue was changed due to the ongoing war in Iran. The men's finals, the ATP Finals, take place from Nov. 15- 22 . The 2026 ATP Finals will be played at Inalpi Arena in Turin, Italy. For these events, singles players and doubles players will be placed into two groups of four. Everyone then plays three round-robin matches, and the top performers advance to the knock-out semifinals and finals. WTA Daily Schedule

 Where to Stream the WTA Finals and ATP Finals 
 While this season's Grand Slam tournaments, including Wimbledon and the US Open , were easy to watch on ESPN, those wishing to tune in for the WTA and ATP Finals won't be so lucky. Instead, Sinclair's Tennis Channel owns the rights to these end-of-season events, so you'll need to subscribe to the standalone streaming service, pay for a cable package that includes the channel, or have access to a live TV streaming service that carries it—and this can get expensive. Tennis Channel : $11.99 per month or $109.99 per year
 DirecTV : Tennis Channel is included with DirecTV's MySports base pack and costs $45 per month for the first six months.
 Fubo : To get the Tennis Channel on Fubo, you'd need to pay for the Elite with Sports Plus tier, which costs $78.99 for the first month.
 Sling : The least expensive way to get Tennis Channel on Sling is to pay for the $46-per-month Orange plan and also get the Sports Extra add-on at $11 per month.
 Hulu + Live TV : If you want the Tennis Channel with Hulu, you'll need to pay the $90 for Live TV, plus the $10-per-month Sports Add-on.
 YouTube TV :  To watch Tennis Channel on YouTube TV, you need to pay $60 per month for the first two months of the base plan, then add the $11.99-per-month NFL RedZone with the Sports Plus Add-on.
 How to Watch the WTA Finals and ATP Finals for Free
 Not looking to pay for yet another subscription? Your options for watching the WTA and ATP Finals for free are limited since the Tennis Channel doesn't offer a free trial. Instead, you're better off signing up for a trial of a live TV service. These trials typically only last a few days, so make sure to time your sign-up correctly so you can watch the matches you want for no extra cost. DirecTV Free Trial - 5 days

 Who Is Playing in the 2026 WTA Finals and ATP Finals?
 The WTA and ATP Finals will feature the season's top eight singles players and doubles teams. Inclusion is determined by a points system in which finishes are scored and weighted by prestige, so a Grand Slam semifinal finish may be worth more points than a win at a lesser tournament. (Credit: WTA Tour) WTA Finals Singles
 This year's top-ranked player is Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan, winner of the Australian Open and US Open. However, Rybakina was forced to withdraw due to an illness. At no. 2, Aryna Sabalenka was the runner-up in these two competitions. Mirra Andreeva (3) won the French Open, and Linda Noskova (8) won at Wimbledon. Americans Jessica Pegula (5) and Coco Gauff (4) have also reached the finals. Here's the full list of ranked competitors, according to the WTA : Aryna Sabalenka

 WTA Finals Doubles
 Gabriela Dabrowski and Luisa Stefani enter the finals as the top-ranked team, having won six competitions this year. At No. 2, the team of Kateřina Siniaková and Taylor Townsend has two Grand Slam victories this season. Other Grand Slam winners include Guo Hanyu and Kristina Mladenovic (3) and Elise Mertens and Zhang Shuai (7). Here's the full list of ranked teams: Gabriela Dabrowski / Luisa Stefani

 ATP Finals Singles
 (Credit: ATP Tour) Following Jannik Sinner's injury earlier in the year, the men's competition became wide open. Alexander Zverev is the top-ranked ATP player, having won at the French Open and US Open. Carlos Alcaraz ranks behind him after a victory at the Australian Open. Americans Ben Shelton (3) and Frances Tiafoe (7) also had big showings this year. Alexander Zverev

 ATP Finals Doubles
 The men's doubles rankings have Harri Heliövaara and Henry Patten at the top after a win at Wimbledon this year. However, the No. 2-ranked team of Christian Harrison and Neal Skupski actually won more Grand Slams, having won in Australia and the US. The third-ranked team of Marcel Granollers and Horacio Zeballos won at the French Open. Harri Heliövaara / Henry Patten

 About Our Expert
 Jason Cohen

 My Experience
 As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
 I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
 The Technology I Use
 My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
 My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. 
 Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.
